claims.claim: The roadmap's "First class support for ApplicationSet resources" entry states that ordered or automated deletion of ApplicationSet children will not be implemented and that teardown remains a manual operator action performed one Application at a time, while the PRD ships exactly that capability as a `deletionOrder` field on `ApplicationSetStrategy` taking `AllAtOnce`/`Reverse`. The design consequence is that the one roadmap item that would have given deletion order a UI/CLI/API surface is the item that explicitly excludes it, so the shipped field has no interface: the only way a user expresses deletion order is by hand-editing the ApplicationSet YAML, and the UI that manages ApplicationSets first-class will show a teardown it cannot control or explain.

The PRD places `deletionOrder` inside `ApplicationSetStrategy`, next to `rollingSync`, so ordering is scoped to the steps of a single ApplicationSet; T-24578 is asking for destroy ordering across multiple ApplicationSets deploying to one cluster, where the deletion ordering of the resulting Applications is "shadowed" by the ApplicationSets. The PRD therefore does not shorten T-24578's path at all: that user still has to build an app-of-apps Application per cluster with a custom Helm chart that re-implements ApplicationSet conditional templating, purely to get sync-wave ordering. The interface answer to "deprovision this cluster in order" remains an indirection layer the user builds themselves.

The PRD's Implementation Details promise validation for exactly one case — `Reverse` selected without a rollingSync order should error out — while the Non-Goals state that the `custom` value will be accepted by the field and silently ignored with no UI statement that it is unavailable. T-28511's reproduction shows how operators actually set this: `deletionOrder` typed directly into the ApplicationSet manifest, with no console step in the loop. So the only feedback channel for a wrong value is the CRD's own validation, and the PRD deliberately removes it for the one value a user is most likely to try after reading the PRD's own `deletionOrder: Custom` example YAML.

flow-dead-end: T-28511 describes an Application generated by a Progressive Sync ApplicationSet, deleted manually in the Argo CD UI, that sticks flipping between Deleting and Syncing status because a crash-looping resource keeps it Progressing, the reverse deletion order waits for one Application to be fully deleted before moving to the next, and the controller restarts the wave from the top. The screen shows two alternating status badges and nothing else: no way forward (the delete never completes), no way back (the controller re-creates the app), and no statement that a wave is waiting on this Application. The actual exit exists only in note-2's incident runbook — switch the ApplicationSet to AllAtOnce before hand-deleting a child — which is prose in a review note, not an offer on the screen. The screen should name the blocking wave and offer the AllAtOnce switch, or refuse the manual delete with the reason.

flow-dead-end: the PRD's `Reverse` deletion strategy waits for one Application to be fully deleted before moving onto the next, which makes a partially-deleted ApplicationSet a reachable resting state whenever one child stalls. Note-1 records that the hydrator History & Rollback work is deprioritized to next quarter, so there is no automated mechanism to revert manifest changes when progressive sync deletion fails mid-way, leaving the application set inconsistent with the cluster. The user is stranded with some children gone, some present, an ordering the controller will not resume, and the one control they would reach for — rollback — unbuilt. The interface needs to state which step of the reverse order it stopped on and offer either resume-from-step or fall back to AllAtOnce.

flow-dead-end: T-27327 records that the first question new users ask when onboarding onto source hydrator is how rollbacks work, because existing deployments roll back through the app's History & Rollback tab, and under source hydrator the rendered manifests in the git branch are the source of truth with no additional controls on the specific revision of the branch. Note-1 then deprioritizes that work to next quarter. Enabling source hydrator therefore silently voids a control every existing user has already been taught, and the tab stays on screen with no message that its Rollback function does not reach the sync branch. Until the rollback lands, the tab should say that rollback is unavailable under source hydrator and name the manual `git checkout $rollback_revision -- $sync_path` path T-27327 spells out.

flow-dead-end: RFC-002 designs push-to-stage as the mode where manifests are pushed to a branch other than the deployment branch and Argo CD relies on an external system to move changes onto it, and it declares implementing a change promotion system a non-goal. T-26443 reports the state that gap creates: in push-to-stage, when the hydrator sync source changes and auto-sync is on, the app immediately syncs whatever the stage branch last held, which can be very old manifests. There is no "hydrated, awaiting promotion" state anywhere in the interface — the app simply reads Synced against stale content, so the correct-looking badge is the failure. T-26443's own proposal (a timestamp annotation that blocks sync against `hydrator.metadata` older than it) is exactly the missing state made visible.

T-27875 and T-27949 are the same interface defect at opposite ends: both let a comparison result stand in for a sync result. In T-27875 `Status.Sync.Revision` holds the last compared revision rather than the last synced revision, so the controller concludes it already attempted the sync and the app sits OutOfSync indefinitely; in T-27949 the ApplicationSet promotes a child from Waiting back to Healthy because the pre-update child was still Synced/Healthy, and the rollout then reports complete while children are OutOfSync. In both, the status a user reads as "this was deployed" only ever meant "this was compared," and in both the user's next move — waiting — is the wrong one, with nothing on screen to say so.

T-27949's rollout reports complete while `status.applicationStatus` stays Healthy and no sync operation is created, because `syncDesiredApplications` only syncs Applications in Pending; the ticket also notes that with the ApplicationSet controller at warn level no progressive-sync transition logs were emitted at all. T-27846 states the matching gap in the product's own words: there is no way to get a wide-eye view of progressive sync, and specifically no answer to "my sync is not starting, why/which Applications is it waiting for?" So the one question a stalled progressive sync forces the user to ask has no surface in the UI and no fallback in the logs — the requested metrics are the missing screen.

T-27949 records that on a repository piloting the source hydrator, every hydration cycle lands a fresh commit on the hydrated branch that the child Applications deploy from and each is picked up as a source change; note-2 confirms the consequence from the incident review, that each hydrator push restarts the rolling sync wave, and sets the interim rule that hydrator pilot repos must not use progressive sync until a debounce exists. To a user watching a RollingSync progress through its steps, this appears as the step indicator jumping back to the first step with no event, no message, and no named cause — the two features that produced it never appear together on any screen. The restriction that would prevent it lives in a review note asking that the pilot ticket carry it, not in any control that refuses the combination.

T-26271's reporter sees a fatal missing-permissions error naming `user "system:serviceaccount:argocd:argocd-server"` and states plainly that the cluster Secret credential is broad and they do not understand why the diff suddenly runs with a narrower identity; note-1 gives the root cause, that with impersonation enabled the diff runs as the destination service account, which does not hold patch on cluster-scoped resources. The defect is that the error text carries the resulting identity but never names the setting that selected it, so nothing on the failure path connects it back to the impersonation flag the team recently enabled on those projects — which is why the reporter goes hunting through the cluster Secret instead. The message needs to name the impersonation setting and the AppProject `destinationServiceAccounts` match that produced the identity.

flow-dead-end: T-28695 describes an external-cluster Application where sync succeeds by impersonating the mapped `destinationServiceAccounts` SA while Server-Side Diff runs as the narrow cluster-Secret credential and fails, so the App rotates Synced to Unknown on every reconcile. Note-1 records the standing decision that impersonation goes behind a per-project flag and that nobody flips it on a project until the diff story is fixed. A user who does flip it lands on a status that changes on a timer with no stable reading, no statement that diff and sync run as different identities, and a workaround (`ServerSideDiff=false`) documented outside the failing screen. The App view should state that diff ran as the cluster credential rather than the impersonated SA and offer the per-Application opt-out inline.

RFC-001 asks the UI to provide an option to create a `DestinationServiceAccount` with `namespace`, `server`, and `defaultServiceAccount` and to add multiple such entries to an AppProject via the web console, and its Special Cases section makes the list order load-bearing: with glob patterns supported on both `server` and `namespace`, the first valid match wins, so `guestbook-*` placed before `*` decides which service account performs the sync. The roadmap says the project management UI evolved organically, was packaged into one sliding panel that is painful to use, and needs a complete redesign, and it schedules the Input Forms UI Refresh only for v2.4 and beyond. A privilege-selecting, order-sensitive, repeating list is therefore being added to the least reorderable surface in the product, with no affordance named anywhere for reordering entries or previewing which service account a given destination resolves to.

T-27833 asks for an Application that can create namespaces dynamically under `CreateNamespace=true` but cannot sync `kind: Namespace` resources committed to the repository, and proposes impersonation with a split — bootstrapping including namespace creation under the Argo CD service account, the sync operation under the impersonated SA. RFC-001 forecloses that shape: the service account for impersonation is determined on a per Application level rather than per resource level, using `Application.spec.destination.namespace` for all resources in the Application, and the feature can be enabled or disabled only at the system level. The interface offers no place to say "this kind, that identity," so the user's stated outcome is unreachable through the impersonation controls the RFC provides.

T-28239 specifies that with `commitserver.sign.hydrated.commits` enabled the commit server fails at startup if the signing key is missing or invalid, refusing to push any commit it cannot verify against the configured key. RFC-002 makes hydration an invisible background step — the application controller notices a new dry commit, queues hydration, and delegates the push to the commit server — with no representation of hydration on the Application beyond the eventual hydrated commit and its README/`hydrator.metadata` output. Combined, a bad signing key produces no error on any Application: the user sees a dry commit land and a hydrated branch that simply stops advancing, with the actual failure confined to a component that never started. The Application needs a hydration state that can read "not hydrated: commit server unavailable," not silence.
